name: Turn-of-the-month effect

origin.source_title: Are Seasonal Anomalies Real? A Ninety-Year Perspective (Review of Financial Studies)

how_it_works.simple: Stocks have tended to rise mostly in the few days around the end and start of each month. So only own stocks on those days.
how_it_works.analogy: Like a shop that does most of its sales on payday weekend; you only open the till then.
how_it_works.precise: Returns over the last trading day of a month and the first three trading days of the next are much higher than on other days. McConnell and Xu (2008) report that over 1926 to 2005 essentially all of the positive US excess market return came in this four-day window, and the effect appears in 31 of 35 countries.

rule: Buy an S&P 500 or total market fund at the close of the second-to-last trading day of the month (so you earn the last trading day) and sell at the close of the third trading day of the new month; hold T-bills otherwise.
economic_rationale: Proposed explanations include month-end pay and pension flows and window dressing, but McConnell and Xu find no support from volume or fund flows, so the cause is unclear.
why_it_might_fail: The edge has shrunk: in the catalog's computation from French daily data, the four-day window averaged 5.4 bp a day versus 4.4 bp on other days over 2008 to 2026, compared with 15.0 bp versus 0.1 bp before 1987.

reported_results.source: McConnell and Xu (2008), working paper abstract on Purdue e-Pubs
reported_results.notes: All of the positive excess market return occurred during the four-day turn-of-the-month interval; on the other 16 days investors received no reward for market risk. No Sharpe figure in the abstract.

reported_results.source: Our calculation from Kenneth French data library, daily market factor
reported_results.notes: Computed by the catalog on 2026-10-20 from the data file at source_url; this exact figure is not printed by the source. Arithmetic mean of monthly returns times 12; volatility is monthly standard deviation times sqrt(12); Sharpe uses excess returns; max drawdown from monthly compounding. Strategy holds the market only on the last and first three trading days of each month, excess return otherwise zero. Turn-of-month days averaged 12.7 bp versus 1.0 bp on other days.

post_publication_evidence: In the catalog's computation from French daily data, the turn-of-month strategy roughly matched buy and hold on a Sharpe basis from 1987 to 2026 (0.59 vs 0.58) and fell well behind it from 2008 to 2026 (0.33 vs 0.67), before costs of about 12 round trips a year. McLean and Pontiff (2016) find that across 97 published stock return predictors, portfolio returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365).

relevance.reason: A simple timing benchmark; a month-end version could be tested on currencies, but these sources only cover stocks.

research.notes: Implemented as `stocks_turn_of_month` and run officially in RUN-000003, but no hypothesis doc yet, so the stage stays at 2 until one is written.
